# How to schedule meetings across time zones

:::answer
Scheduling a meeting across time zones works best when you stop guessing offsets and send a link instead. We built SavvyCal so recipients see your open times in their own time zone and can even overlay their own calendar, so they pick a slot that works rather than one you had to convert by hand.
:::

:::takeaways
- A scheduling link removes manual time zone math for both sides of the meeting.
- Recipients can overlay their own calendar on your SavvyCal link to compare availability at a glance.
- Limiting which slots you offer keeps the meeting from landing at an unreasonable hour for either party.
- Caps on meetings per day or week stop a full calendar of cross-time-zone bookings from crowding out deep work.
- Team scheduling links combine multiple people's availability so group meetings across zones don't take extra emails.
:::

## What do you need before you start?

You need a calendar that reflects your real commitments, since any scheduling tool is only as accurate as the calendar behind it. You also need a scheduling link to send instead of a string of proposed times, because typing out times across zones invites errors and back-and-forth.

If you're scheduling with a team rather than one person, you need everyone's calendars connected to the same tool so their time can be combined into one link. For webinars or group calls where several people will book the same slot, you need a link set up to allow multiple schedulers to join at once rather than one built for one-on-one meetings.

Finally, decide ahead of time which hours you're willing to meet in. [SavvyCal](https://savvycal.com/) points out that just because you're technically “available” doesn’t mean a block should fill with meetings, and that applies doubly when the other person is six or ten hours away and a “convenient” slot for them might be your early morning or late evening.

## What are the steps to schedule across time zones?

Once your calendar and link are ready, the actual scheduling takes a handful of steps, most of which happen on the recipient's side rather than yours.

1. Connect your calendar to your scheduling tool, so your open slots are accurate and update automatically as new events get added.
2. Create a scheduling link rather than listing times manually. SavvyCal replaced the “click-a-day then click-a-time” interface with a week view, so a full week of options is visible at once ([SavvyCal](https://savvycal.com/)).
3. Set your acceptable hours and any limits on meeting load, since SavvyCal lets you prevent meeting overload and cap quantity per day, week, and month ([SavvyCal](https://savvycal.com/)).
4. Send the link to the other person instead of proposing specific times yourself.
5. Let the recipient view the link in their own time zone, which the tool converts automatically, so neither of you is doing the math.
6. Have the recipient overlay their own calendar on your link if they want to compare commitments side by side rather than switching tabs. SavvyCal notes that recipients can overlay their calendar on top of your link to spot ideal times at a glance ([SavvyCal](https://savvycal.com/)).
7. For a meeting with more than one host, combine availability across colleagues on a single link rather than collecting each person's hours by email, something SavvyCal describes as combining your availability with multiple colleagues on scheduling links ([SavvyCal](https://savvycal.com/)).
8. Confirm the booking once the recipient picks a slot, which locks the time on both calendars without a follow-up email.

## How do you check the meeting time is right?

Open the confirmed event on your own calendar and check that the local time shown matches when you expect to be free, since a booking that lands at 11 p.m. your time usually means the link's hours weren't restricted tightly enough. Then check the invite the other person received to confirm it displays in their time zone rather than yours.

If you share the link with people in several regions, book a test slot yourself from a browser set to a different time zone, or ask a colleague in another region to do it, so you can see what they see before a real prospect does. This matters more for group links, since a link combining several team members' hours can produce a narrower overlap than any one person's calendar alone.

Watch for a booking that falls right at the edge of your allowed hours. A slot of 7 a.m. or 9 p.m. technically fits inside a wide availability window but rarely fits inside a reasonable one, which is the gap SavvyCal's quantity caps and time-budgeting features are meant to close ([SavvyCal](https://savvycal.com/)).

## What mistakes should you avoid when scheduling across time zones?

The most common mistake is sending a list of proposed times written in your own time zone and trusting the other person to convert them correctly. SavvyCal observes that not all time slots are created equal, and a slot that looks fine on your calendar can be the worst hour of someone else's day.

### Opening your calendar too wide
Marking yourself available for every daylight hour invites bookings at the far edges of your day once someone several time zones away picks from the full range. Narrow the window to hours you'd want a meeting in, not just hours you're technically free.

### Scheduling one person at a time by hand
Wrangling multiple team members' availability by hand is just plain silly, as SavvyCal puts it, and the problem compounds once those team members sit in different time zones ([SavvyCal](https://savvycal.com/)). A combined link avoids collecting everyone's hours over email.

### Ignoring your own meeting load
Agreeing to every slot a recipient picks, regardless of time zone convenience, can quietly fill a calendar with early or late meetings. SavvyCal's stance is that your calendar shouldn't fill just because a time is technically open, and capping bookings per day or week keeps that from happening.

## Can the person booking see their own calendar?

Yes, the person booking can see their own calendar inside the scheduling link rather than switching between tabs to compare it against yours. SavvyCal says the recipient can view their calendar events on top of your scheduling link, to save them the hassle of clicking back and forth, which matters most when they're also juggling a time zone conversion in their head ([SavvyCal](https://savvycal.com/)).
